### 4.2.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law and the Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

Facing the reality of this massive cognitive disruption, civil law must not remain rigid and conservative by clinging to a narrow interpretation of Article 1321 in conjunction with Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*) concerning defects of will (*vitiated consent*). A radical yet systematic doctrinal reconstruction is required to expand the scope of mistake (*dwaling*) and fraud (*bedrog*) so that they can encompass the realities of human-machine interaction. This novel construction must recognize that individual autonomy in the digital age is no longer independently self-contained, but rather relational and distributed. Consequently, the law must introduce the concept of **Algorithmic-Induced Mistake** (*Algorithmic-Induced Dwaling*) as a legitimate and legally weighty ground to demand the voidability of an agreement (*vernietigbaarheid*), without being burdened by traditional standards of proof that ignore the asymmetries of digital information.

Within this framework of doctrinal reconstruction, the burden of proof for the criterion of excusable mistake (*verschoonbare dwaling*) must be reversed. If a transaction arises from interaction with an autonomous agent or an AI system utilizing hyper-personalization framing techniques and emotional manipulation, the law must formulate a rebuttable presumption that the mistake experienced by the consumer is excusable, unless the technology provider can prove otherwise—namely, that their system operates transparently, neutrally, and provides substantial information that is fully accessible and reasonably understandable to the average person. The doctrine of undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*), which has hitherto been applied primarily within traditional power dynamics (such as doctor-patient or attorney-client relationships), must be expanded analogously to encompass the relationship between AI system architects and end-users who find themselves in cognitively vulnerable positions.

Furthermore, personal data protection instruments such as the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) (*UU PDP*), particularly the provisions concerning the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing (*automated decision-making*), must be organically integrated into the civil law doctrine regarding the validity of contracts (Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code). Any agreement born from algorithmic latent space tuning that is proven to distort the essence of free will must be categorized as containing a fundamental defect of will, granting the injured party the right to rescind the contract and demand the restoration of the status quo (*restitutio in integrum*) along with damages for psychological and material losses suffered.

The reconstruction of individual sovereignty in the era of artificial intelligence demands that civil law transform from a merely passive, neutral referee into a proactive guardian of substantive justice. The law must recognize that contractual freedom will lose its moral significance if human will itself is reduced to mere numerical variables within the predictive algorithms of Big Tech corporations. By redefining mistake (*dwaling*) as a distortion of reality born from systemic information engineering, we not only rescue individual victims from the snares of invisible digital traps, but we also reaffirm human dignity within the bulwark of a sovereign, just, and dignified civil legal system.

Any agreement arising from the adjustment of an algorithmic latent space distorted by the illusion of intimacy necessitates a radical re-reading of what we understand as "free will" in the presence of machines (Hildebrandt, 2015; Calo, 2014).
